entries.title: How to Prevent Poisoned GitHub Actions Dependencies
entries.source: freeCodeCamp Programming Tutorials: Python, JavaScript, Git & More
entries.content:
Your workflow uses `actions/checkout@v4`. Today, that tag points to a vetted release. Tomorrow, a compromised maintainer or attacker moves the tag to malicious code. Your pipeline runs it with access to `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

Third-party **Actions are dependencies**. A floating tag behaves like an unpinned package dependency. If the reference changes, the workflow can execute different code without any change to your repository.

This article shows you how to prevent poisoned continuous integration (CI) dependencies by pinning Actions to full commit SHAs, validating those pins against release tags, restricting permitted actions, and automating reviewed updates with Dependabot.

**Who this is for:** Platform and DevSecOps engineers securing GitHub Actions workflows.

**Prerequisites:**

* Repository admin access
* Workflows using `uses: org/action@ref` syntax

## The Quick Reference:

Here's what you'll learn how to do here:

* Pin every `uses:` reference to a **full commit SHA**, not a moving tag such as `@v4`.
* Validate that each recorded SHA matches the release you reviewed before approving it.
* Maintain an **allowlist** of permitted actions at the organization or repository level.
* Enable **Dependabot** for GitHub Actions version bumps with review.
* Prefer official or verified creators. Mirror critical actions internally if needed.
* Verify pins in pull request checks before merge.

## Table of Contents

* [The Quick Reference](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-the-quick-reference)
* [Why Floating Tags Fail](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-why-floating-tags-fail)
* [Pin Actions to Commit SHAs](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-pin-actions-to-commit-shas)
* [Validate the Commit SHAs](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-validate-the-commit-shas)
* [Enable Dependabot for Actions](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-enable-dependabot-for-actions)
* [Allowlist Actions](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-allowlist-actions)
* [Enforce Pins in Pull Requests](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-enforce-pins-in-pull-requests)
* [Vet Third-Party Actions](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-vet-third-party-actions)
* [How to Verify This Works](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-how-to-verify-this-works)
* [When This Breaks Down](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-when-this-breaks-down)
* [Conclusion](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-conclusion)
* [References](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-prevent-poisoned-github-actions-dependencies/#heading-references)

## Why Floating Tags Fail

GitHub Actions lets you reference a dependency with a branch name, version tag, or commit SHA. These references don't provide the same level of stability. A branch can change at any time, and a version tag can be moved to a different commit after you review it. A commit SHA identifies one specific revision.

The table below compares the common reference styles and shows why a moving tag creates a supply chain risk:

| Reference style | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `@main` | Runs whatever code is on the branch when the workflow starts |
| `@v4` | The tag can move, so the same label can execute different code |
| `@v4.2.1` | More specific, but still a mutable tag |
| `@abc1234...` (full SHA) | Identifies one immutable commit |

The first three references fail because the name doesn't permanently identify the code that GitHub will execute. A full SHA solves that specific problem by making the workflow change only when someone changes the reference in the repository.

**Key idea:** CI pipelines deserve the same dependency discipline as application code.

## Pin Actions to Commit SHAs

Pinning an Action means replacing its branch or version tag with the full SHA of the commit you reviewed. GitHub then checks out that exact revision, even if the publisher later moves the original tag.

This first example is **bad** because both references use mutable version tags. The workflow may run different Action code later without a corresponding change in your repository:

```
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
```

This second example is **good** because each reference uses a full 40-character commit SHA. The comments preserve the readable release versions for maintainers, but GitHub uses the SHA rather than the comments:

```
- uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
- uses: actions/setup-node@4992456781334f2795ae9dd169f5041797d85689 # v4.4.0
```

Find the SHA on the action's GitHub release page or:

```
gh api repos/actions/checkout/git/ref/tags/v4.2.2 --jq '.object.sha'
```

Use the exact release tag you reviewed. Add a comment with the human-readable version for maintainability. The comment helps a reviewer, but it's not part of the security control. GitHub executes the commit identified by the SHA.

Don't use a shortened SHA. A full 40-character SHA makes accidental collisions and ambiguous reviews less likely.

## Validate the Commit SHAs

A full SHA protects the workflow from a tag moving after you merge it, but you still need to validate the SHA before approving it. The release tag and commit should be reviewed together. This check compares the commit behind the reviewed tag with the commit recorded in the workflow:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

repository="actions/checkout"
release_tag="v4.2.2"
expected_sha="11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683"

actual_sha="$({
  git ls-remote "https://github.com/${repository}.git" \
    "refs/tags/${release_tag}" "refs/tags/${release_tag}^{}"
} | awk -v tag="refs/tags/${release_tag}" '
  $2 == tag "^{}" { print $1; found = 1 }
  $2 == tag { fallback = $1 }
  END { if (!found) print fallback }
')"

if [[ "${actual_sha}" != "${expected_sha}" ]]; then
  printf 'SHA mismatch for %s %s\n' "${repository}" "${release_tag}" >&2
  printf 'Expected: %s\nActual:   %s\n' "${expected_sha}" "${actual_sha}" >&2
  exit 1
fi

printf 'Validated %s@%s\n' "${repository}" "${expected_sha}"
```

This is release-reference validation, not a claim that a repository is trustworthy. Read the action source, review its permissions, and record why you approved the dependency. For higher-assurance environments, mirror critical actions internally and validate the mirrored artifact through your normal repository controls.

## Enable Dependabot for Actions

Dependabot is GitHub's automated dependency-update service. For GitHub Actions, it checks the workflow references for newer releases and opens pull requests that update them. This gives you a reviewable place to inspect and approve an Action update instead of changing pins manually or using floating tags.

Create `.github/dependabot.yml`:

```
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    groups:
      actions:
        patterns:
          - "*"
```

Dependabot opens pull requests when pinned SHAs have newer releases. Review and merge like application dependencies.

Don't configure Dependabot to merge these updates automatically until you have a review process for action changes. An update can contain new permissions, changed scripts, or a new transitive dependency.

For each update pull request, compare the old and new commit, inspect the action's release notes, and review changes to `action.yml` JavaScript bundles, shell scripts, and workflow permissions. Confirm that the new commit belongs to the release you intended to adopt. Run the workflow in a test repository or environment when the action handles deployment, publishing, credentials, or other high-impact operations.

The goal isn't to reject every update. The goal is to make the trust decision visible and repeatable. A reviewer should be able to answer three questions before merging: what code changed, why is the new version needed, and what permissions can that code use?

## Allowlist Actions

An Action allowlist is a repository or organization policy that limits which publishers and repositories workflows are allowed to call. It reduces the chance that a contributor introduces an unknown or unreviewed Action into a trusted pipeline.

Organization administrators can configure it at **Settings → Actions → Policies → Allow specified actions**. Choose the narrowest policy that matches your workflows, then add only the Action repositories your teams have reviewed.

Example allowlist patterns:

```
actions/checkout@*
actions/setup-node@*
actions/cache@*
docker/*
my-org/*
```

With this policy, Actions that don't match the approved patterns are denied. Repositories under the organization inherit the policy, subject to the organization's GitHub plan and repository settings.

For a single repo without an org policy, use **Settings → Actions → General → Allow actions created by GitHub, and select non-GitHub actions** and restrict to verified creators only.

An allowlist limits which action identities may run. It doesn't replace SHA pinning. A permitted action should still be referenced by a reviewed full SHA in every workflow.

## Enforce Pins in Pull Requests

Run a workflow linter in CI and add a repository check that fails when a workflow introduces a non-SHA reference. Pin the checker itself before using it in a protected workflow. Replace the placeholder below with the full commit SHA you verified for the actionlint release you selected:

```
name: actionlint

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683
      - uses: rhysd/actionlint@03d0035246f3e81f36aed592ffb4bebf33a03106 # v1.7.7
        with:
          args: -color
```

Resolve the release tag, review the commit, and record the full 40-character SHA just as you did for `actions/checkout`.

You can also use a small check to catch common floating references. Treat this as a backup signal, not a YAML parser or a complete supply chain policy:

```
      - name: Reject floating action tags
        run: |
          if grep -RInE '^[[:space:]]*-?[[:space:]]*uses:[[:space:]]*[^#]+@(main|master|v[0-9]+)([[:space:]]|$)' .github/workflows/; then
            echo "Floating action refs found. Pin to full SHA."
            exit 1
          fi
```

The check should run on pull requests and on protected branches. A pull request can pass this test and still contain a malicious commit, so combine it with code review, the allowlist, and the SHA validation process.

## Vet Third-Party Actions

Before adding a community action to the allowlist:

1. Read the action's `action.yml` and entry script.
2. Check star history, maintainer reputation, and open security issues.
3. Pin SHA and fork to `my-org/action-name` if the action is critical but externally maintained.

Also inspect the permissions available to the workflow. An action that can read repository secrets or write releases deserves more scrutiny than an action that only formats a file. Set the workflow's top-level permissions to the minimum required, then grant additional permissions to individual jobs only when needed.

## How to Verify This Works

1. Run the SHA validation script for every action you approve and expect all comparisons to pass.
2. Open a test pull request that changes an action to`@main`, and confirm the CI gate fails.
3. Add a trailing comment after a floating tag and confirm your parser or linter still rejects it.
4. Confirm organization policy blocks a disallowed action in a test workflow.
5. Confirm Dependabot opens an action update pull request and that the change receives normal review.
6. Review the workflow run permissions and verify that the action can't access credentials it doesn't need.

## When This Breaks Down

1. **Emergency patches:** SHA pinning slows hotfixes. Dependabot plus on-call review is safer than temporarily using a floating tag.
2. **Composite actions in private repos:** pin internal actions the same way as public ones.
3. **Reusable workflows:** pin the reusable workflow ref to SHA as well as steps inside it.
4. **Annotated tags and mirrors:** resolve annotated tags to their commit before recording a SHA, and validate internal mirrors through your own change-control process.
5. **False sense of safety:** pinning without reading code still trusts the maintainer at pin time. Combine pinning with allowlists, least-privilege permissions, and review.

## Conclusion

In this tutorial, you learned how to prevent poisoned CI dependencies by pinning GitHub Actions to reviewed commit SHAs, validating those references, allowlisting trusted actions, enabling Dependabot updates, and enforcing pins in pull request checks.

The result is a layered control: a reviewed immutable reference, a restricted set of permitted actions, automated update proposals, and a pull request check that catches regressions before merge.

## References

* [GitHub Actions, Security hardening](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions)
* [GitHub, Dependabot version updates for Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot/working-with-dependabot/keeping-your-actions-up-to-date-with-dependabot)
* [StepSecurity, Pin GitHub Actions](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security)
* [OpenSSF, Source compromise defenses](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/main/docs/checks.md#pinned-dependencies)

entries.title: Do the Apple Watch Series 12's New Health Features Live Up to the Hype?
entries.content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

I now have the [Apple Watch Series 12](https://zdcs.link/9ZJjmm?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Apple%20Watch%20Series%2012&object_type=content&short_url=9ZJjmm&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") in my hands—or, rather, on my wrist—and have spent the past 24 hours putting it through as many tests as I can manage. I'm pleased with the step counting and the availability of "recovery HRV" (as opposed to the cardiac-health-focused HRV that the Apple Watch previously used) but I'm not sure if the heart rate accuracy is living up to the hype. I'll be putting this device to more rigorous tests, but here are my first thoughts.

[Apple Watch Series 12

$399.00
at Amazon

Learn More

![Apple Watch Series 12](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/product/01CpisyU0qXURsN7TKwXYh0/hero-image.fill.size_autoxauto.v1789651012.jpg)

![Apple Watch Series 12](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/product/01CpisyU0qXURsN7TKwXYh0/hero-image.fill.size_autoxauto.v1789651012.jpg)

Learn More

$399.00
at Amazon](https://cc.lifehacker.com/v1/otc/06ZVRiLmglGs4QA6plTXzTC?merchant=05kie42h3YvHwjr4G1w80Qq&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2Fdp%2FB0HJBCX8VS&template=article&module=shop-card&element=offer&item=offer-btn&position=1&element_label=Apple+Watch+Series+12&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss&product_uuid=01CpisyU0qXURsN7TKwXYh0&offer_uuid=02CCzxbQ1nZMAWX7Q04JlTe&object_type=article&object_uuid=01M2TSPPTN4Y9KVTK5H0WJVH5Y&pageview_type=RSS&data-aps-asin=B0HJBCX8VS&data-aps-asc-tag=lifehack088-20&data-aps-asc-subtag=01M2TSPPTN4Y9KVTK5H0WJVH5Y "(opens in a new window)")

![Backs of two Apple watches showing the different appearance of their sensors](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/articles/01M2TSPPTN4Y9KVTK5H0WJVH5Y/images-1.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789753252.jpg)

Apple redesigned the heart rate sensor on the back of the watch. Left: Apple Watch Series 11. Right: Apple Watch Series 12
Credit: Beth Skwarecki

## Step counting is everything I hoped it would be

Apple waited forever to add step counting as an easily viewable metric on the watch, but it’s finally here. I can open my smart stack (with a double pinch of my fingers, not even touching the watch screen) and see my steps right on top. I’ve also added a step count complication to my watch face. You can find this complication under **Activity**. The option to see your rings as a complication is still there, but you can now also add steps or wheelchair pushes.

Step counts work well. They update quickly, and seem to be accurate in my casual counting—nine steps from my desk to the door registers as nine steps. I’ll do more in-depth testing soon, to properly evaluate Apple’s claim that it now has the most accurate step counting out there.

What’s disappointing is that it took so long—and that step counting is not coming to the Series 11 or any earlier watch. Apple’s step counting uses a special pedometer model that’s built into its new processor. Older Apple watches don’t have the hardware to calculate your steps as precisely, leading Apple to leave the feature off those watches. That is wild to me, considering that every other wearable has had step counts on the watch ever since the first cave dweller strapped a rock to their wrist.

## I’m not sure I buy these “most accurate heart rate” claims

Apple claims the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate in a wearable, and I’ve already [mentioned](https://lifehacker.com/health/apple-health-app-redesign) that that's a bold claim given what I’ve seen in the past from Apple and from other devices. Now that I have a Series 12 in my hands, I was able to do some preliminary testing.

To be totally clear, these are *not* thorough tests, and I’m not making a decisive conclusion based on just a few days’ testing. But I’ll show you what I’ve tried so far.

As always, I’m testing the device against my heart rate as read by a chest strap (the gold standard for heart rate comparisons). I did:

* A treadmill interval run with the Series 11 and a chest strap
* An identical treadmill interval run with the Series 12, a chest strap, and the [Garmin Forerunner 570](https://zdcs.link/QbbNYE?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Garmin%20Forerunner%20570&object_type=content&short_url=QbbNYE&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") for good measure
* An outdoor run that included steady jogging, intervals, and walking, with the Series 12, a chest strap, and the 570.

I’m including the 570 in these tests because it has what *I* would consider the most accurate heart rate sensor in a wearable. In my [past testing](https://lifehacker.com/health/garmin-forerunner-570-review) it’s reported numbers that were identical or nearly identical to the chest strap. That said, there’s always variation from day to day, and it didn’t shine quite as well in these recent tests compared to some I’ve done in the past.

![Apple Watch Series 11 and 12 vs chest strap](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/articles/01M2TSPPTN4Y9KVTK5H0WJVH5Y/images-2.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789753252.png)

Apple Watch Series 11, top, and 12, bottom. Red dots are the Apple Watches; gray is the chest strap for reference.
Credit: Beth Skwarecki

Here are the indoor runs with the Series 11 on top, and the Series 12 on the bottom, both in red and both compared to a chest strap. The Series 11 was already doing a pretty good job, and to be honest I’m not sure if the Series 12 is any better. I’m disappointed that the Series 12 is still only sampling heart rate every five seconds during workouts. Other devices, like the chest strap and the Garmin, sample every second. That means Apple is taking 12 data points every minute while these other devices are taking 60.

![Graph of outdoor workout; see text for interpretation](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/articles/01M2TSPPTN4Y9KVTK5H0WJVH5Y/images-3.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789753392.png)

Apple Watch Series 12 in red, Garmin Forerunner 570 in blue, chest strap for reference in gray
Credit: Beth Skwarecki

Here’s the outdoor run. The chest strap is in gray, Garmin in blue, and Apple in red. Again, the sparse data points of the Apple watch aren’t impressive. I see a few places where Apple missed the peak of a small spike, but then again the Garmin struggled in a few spots as well. I’ll do further testing and report back when I’ve been able to try out the watch in a greater variety of activities and conditions.

## What I can’t test yet

Live Rewind and Siri Recaps aren’t available yet. Live Rewind is the feature where you can ask for a text transcription of whatever was said around you in the last 15 seconds. Recaps handle a longer timeframe—for example, to summarize a meeting. These features are coming later this year, and aren’t in the version of watchOS 27 that came with the watch. (I have not installed any beta software on the watch.)

Readiness is another big feature coming soon, but I haven’t logged enough nights of sleep to get my scores yet—it needs about a week of data. As a preview, I am seeing my “recovery HRV” listed with my sleep data. Last night my HRV was 45 according to Apple, and 50 according to my Oura ring. HRV readings from different devices may vary, depending on exactly when they take their measurements, so I’ll be looking for trends rather than specific data points. If both devices agree on what is a high or a low reading for me, given my baseline, I’ll call that a success for Apple.

If you're planning on giving home entertainment gear as a gift this holiday, forget about traditional benchmarks like "biggest screen" or "most expensive speakers." Match the gear with the personality and needs of the person being entertained by that home entertainment system instead. Below are my best picks for everyone from college kids squeezed in a dorm room to legacy media snobs for whom streaming video isn't an option.

## Best overall home entertainment gift of 2026: Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box 8K

You probably won't buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can give the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing watching and gaming is the mission of the [Philips Hue Play Sync Box](https://zdcs.link/QL26d0?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Philips%20Hue%20Play%20Sync%20Box&object_type=content&short_url=QL26d0&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window"). It’s a middleman between TVs and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for gaming immersion, but it also improves just watching TV. Projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals gives the illusion of a bigger screen, and it's just cool.

entries.title: Gyazo Data Breach Exposes 23 Million User Records
entries.content:
## A Gyazo breach exposed 23 million user records after attackers exploited a vulnerability in Helpfeel’s image upload server.

Japanese software company Helpfeel is notifying Gyazo users about a data breach that compromised 23 million user records. Attackers gained unauthorized access by exploiting a vulnerability in the service’s image upload server.

“We have confirmed that approximately 23.62 million records containing data related to Gyazo users were disclosed without authorization.” *[notice of data breach](https://corp.helpfeel.com/en/news/news-20260916).*

Gyazo is a popular cross-platform tool for capturing screenshots, GIFs and short screen recordings and instantly sharing them through links. The incident highlights the risks of vulnerabilities in systems that handle and store user-generated content.

Helpfeel said this week that it recently discovered unauthorized access to its Gyazo servers. The threat actor exploited a vulnerability in the image upload server on September 11 and was able to run malicious commands.

The attacker was locked out the following day, but had already accessed a database containing about 23.6 million user records.

The stolen data includes names, email addresses, password hashes, user and device IDs, X integration tokens, profile details, usage statistics and billing information.

Helpfeel said payment card data was not affected.

*“Helpfeel Inc. (Head Office: Kyoto, Japan; Representative Director and CEO: Isshu Rakusai; hereinafter “Helpfeel”) has confirmed that Gyazo, our image-sharing service, was subject to unauthorized access by a third party, resulting in the unauthorized disclosure of user information and certain metadata associated with uploaded images.” continues the [notice of data breach](https://corp.helpfeel.com/en/news/news-20260916). “We have blocked all access routes used in the incident and have completed remediation of the vulnerability that was exploited. We continue to prioritize measures to prevent further harm while investigating the scope and impact of the incident.”*

Helpfeel confirmed that exposed data may include names or nicknames, email addresses, password hashes, user IDs, device IDs, login session IDs, X integration tokens, Google SSO email addresses, profile information, language preferences, registration and last login dates and times, subscription plans, billing status, and usage statistics.

The affected records also include anonymous accounts without registered email addresses. Helpfeel said no payment information, including credit card numbers, was exposed. The investigation is still ongoing, so further details may emerge.

The company also confirmed that about 490 million image metadata records were exposed, mainly linked to images uploaded in or before January 2019. Metadata from another 2.4 million images was also accessed through specific searches. The exposed information may include image IDs, upload IP addresses, User-Agent data, EXIF location information, OCR text, image titles, source URLs, other metadata and hashed passphrases for private images.

Some of this information could potentially be used to reconstruct Gyazo image URLs and access images without authorization. The company temporarily disabled access to some images and confirmed that a list of private images was obtained. It has not confirmed that image files themselves were stolen, but cannot rule out that some private images were viewed. No unauthorized disclosure has been confirmed in Helpfeel or Cosense systems.

*“We plan to send notifications regarding this incident to the registered email addresses of Gyazo users who may have been affected. We are currently working to identify users whose information was disclosed without authorization and will determine which users to notify based on the progress of our investigation.” continues the notice. “For users we are unable to reach by email, such as those with anonymous accounts without a registered email address or similar contact information, we plan to provide notifications through the Gyazo web interface.”*

The investigation is still ongoing, and the company will publish updates if further information emerges. The company is asking all Gyazo users to change their passwords, especially if the same or a similar password is used on other services. Users should also stay alert for suspicious emails, messages or other communications that may attempt to exploit the breach.

These precautions are intended to reduce the risk of further account compromise or phishing attacks.

entries.title: Virginia governor creates an AI task force and moves to restrain data centers
entries.content:
![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/gettyimages-2295948062.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) [ordered the state government](https://www.governor.virginia.gov//newsroom/news-releases/2026/september-releases/name-1123696-en.html) to take steps that could empower local communities to have a larger say in data center development and slow down approvals in a state that is already home to the [data center capital of the world](https://www.theverge.com/cs/features/975597/loudoun-county-virginia-data-center-backlash).

The order also establishes an AI task force responsible for evaluating how the state government can address risks to Virginians like …

entries.title: NASA Invites Media to Albania Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony
entries.content:
[![NASA meatball](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/cropped-nasa-meatball-1.jpg?w=1080)](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/cropped-nasa-meatball-1.jpg)

Credit: NASA

The Republic of Albania will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 12 p.m. EDT on Monday, Sept. 21, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 73rd country signatory.

NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson will host Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha and Ambassador of the Republic of Albania to the United States Ervin Bushati for the ceremony, together with U.S. Department of State officials.

This event is in person only. Media interested in attending must RSVP no later than 10 a.m. on Sept. 21 to: [hq-media@mail.nasa.gov](mailto:hq-media@mail.nasa.gov). NASA’s [media accreditation policy](https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasa-agencywide-media-accreditation-policy/) is online.

In 2020, during the first Trump Administration, the United States, led by NASA and the State Department, joined with seven other founding nations to establish the Artemis Accords, responding to the growing interest in lunar activities by both governments and private companies.

The Artemis Accords introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety, transparency, and coordination of civil space exploration on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Learn more about the Artemis Accords at:

[**https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-accords**](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-accords)

entries.title: The Fat Bear Week 2026 bracket is here and chunkier than ever
entries.content:
It’s almost time! The official [Fat Bear Week 2026](https://www.popsci.com/environment/fat-bear-week-2026-begins-september-22/) bracket has landed, and this year’s competition will see 16 adult brown bears (*Ursus arctos*) in Alaska go head-to-head in the bracket-style online competition.

In group one are the mother bears, including:

* First-timer Bear #132 and her spring cubs,
* A bear with a long lineage at Katmai designated as [Bear #284 (Electra)](https://www.popsci.com/environment/katmai-brown-bear-cubs-walk-water-alaska/) and her two cubs
* [Bear #806](http://google.com/url?q=https://www.popsci.com/environment/bear-cub-killed-katmai-brooks-river-bear-806/&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1789762704452457&usg=AOvVaw0G6tzsFT_Tn12BAgkw1BAI) and her mixed age cubs
* Bear #901 and her spring cub

In group two are the single adult females, including:

* The resilient [Bear #909](https://www.popsci.com/environment/bear-cub-killed-katmai-brooks-river-bear-806/) (who lost two of her cubs this season)
* Bear #428 (the descendant of a former Fat Bear Week champion named Bear #128 Grazer)
* 9-year-old Bear #113 (aka Marshmallow)
* [Bear #910](https://www.popsci.com/environment/katmai-blended-family-adopted-bears-609-620/) (a member of a [history-making blended bear family](https://www.popsci.com/environment/bear-910-fat-bear-week-contender-2026/))

In group 3, we have the sub-adults bears:

* First-timer Bear #694
* A sub-adult on the cusp of adulthood designed as [Bear #620](https://www.popsci.com/environment/katmai-blended-family-adopted-bears-609-620/)
* The resilient Bear #610
* Crowd-favorite Bear #89 (Backpack) who is the son of Bear #435 Holly

And finally, in group four, the behemoth adult male bears:

* [2025 Fat Bear Week Champion Bear #32 (Chunk)](https://www.popsci.com/environment/chunk-returns-ahead-of-fat-bear-week-2026/)
* Young upstart and [ace fisher-bear designated as Bear #164 (Bucky Dent)](https://www.popsci.com/environment/meet-bucky-dent-one-of-katmais-most-innovative-fish-finder/)
* Bear #151 (Walker)
* Bear #903 (Gully)

In addition to being digital competitors in this online tournament, Bear #151 and Bear #903 have proven to be real-life competitors, often going after the same salmon.

![a bracket of bears](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026-fat-bear-week-bracket.png?strip=all&quality=85)

The 2026 Fat Bear Week Bracket. *Image: explore.org.*

According to Katmai National Park and Preserve naturalist Mike Fitz, the brown bears have reached “peak fat” and are ready to handle the long salmon-less winter ahead. Over 100 different bears were identified at Katmai’s Brooks River this summer, and not all of them could be included in the competition. The team at Katmai selected from bears who showed up at the river early in the summer and re-appeared again later in the season. This allowed the team to take good before-and-after photos that show off how much weight they packed on while feasting on salmon over the summer.

[Fat Bear Week begins on Tuesday, September 22](https://explore.org/fat-bear-week), and a winner will be crowned on Tuesday, September 29. Voters can continue to get to know Katmai’s iconic bears via explore.org’s livestream and highlight reels.

Here is everything you need to know to prepare for this year’s celebration of Alaska’s chunky predators:

---

## What is Fat Bear Week?

Think March Madness, just without the basketball and significantly more bears. Fat Bear Week is a single-elimination tournament, where [bear enthusiasts from around the world can vote online for their favorite chunky bear](https://katmaiconservancy.org/fatbearweek). After each round, the bear with the most votes advances until the winner is announced. According to the Katmai Conservancy, the event began as a one-day event in 2014 with 1,700 votes cast. Only 10 years later, 1.2 million votes were cast from over 100 countries.

The brown bears [return to Brooks Falls for the salmon migration](https://www.nps.gov/katm/learn/nature/bears-of-katmai.htm) every year in late June, where viewers can watch them on [explore.org](http://explore.org)’s livestream. There, they will feast to fatten up for the long winter ahead. By late summer, the nutritious fish will spawn and then begin to die. The bears will then move to the lower Brooks River in September and October to eat the dead and dying salmon near the river’s mouth.

Eating all of this salmon is important because the heftier the bear, the better chance they will survive their long winter hibernation. Despite being the poster species for winter hibernation, bears are [not “deep hibernators,”](https://www.popsci.com/environment/how-animals-stay-warm-winter/) they way that squirrels, bats, and bees are. [Bears enter a state called torpor](https://www.popsci.com/environment/do-bears-hibernate/), which is an involuntary state primarily triggered by lack of food. During this time, the bears rely on stored fat reserves for energy. A torpid bear’s eating, drinking, and waste functions will cease, as its body metabolizes these stores it put on over the summer.

## When is Fat Bear Week 2026?

This year, [Fat Bear Week begins on Tuesday, September 22](https://explore.org/fat-bear-week), and a winner will be crowned on Tuesday, September 29.

## How can I vote?

Votes may be cast from 12 p.m. to 9 p.m. EDT (9 a.m. to 6 p.m. PDT and 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ADT)

from September 22 and 29 at [fatbearweek.org](http://fatbearweek.org).

Photographs comparing the bears from earlier in the summer and later in the summer will be shown, so voters can get an idea of just how much weight the bears put on during their salmon fest. An adult male bear can go from [roughly 700 pounds in the early summer to over 1,200 pounds by fall.](https://www.outsideonline.com/outdoor-adventure/environment/why-do-fat-bears-get-so-fat/) Voters are also encouraged to get familiar with each bear’s life history and the unique challenges they face to survive.

## Which bears are competing this year?

This year’s competition includes 16 adult brown bears separated into four main groups—mother bears, single females (those who do not have cubs), sub-adults, and adult males.

In 2025, [Bear #32 (Chunk) took the crown](https://www.popsci.com/environment/fat-bear-week-champion-chunk-alaska/), despite beginning the salmon run with a freshly broken jaw. He was likely injured while fighting with another bear for a mate, but he still managed to catch plenty of fish. Chunk is [known for his dominance and size](https://explore.org/meet-the-bears), but also narrow-set eyes, dark fur, a prominent brow ridge, and a distinctive scar across his muzzle.

Chunk wasn’t always a fan favorite though. In 2024, he lost the Fat Bear Week crown for the second year in a row to [mama bear Grazer](https://www.popsci.com/environment/fat-bear-week-winner-2023/). The two bears had been involved in an incident in which two of Grazer’s 2024 cubs were attacked by Chunk after falling over a waterfall. [Grazer put up a fight against Chunk](https://www.npr.org/2024/10/09/nx-s1-5147101/fat-bear-week-winner-2024) to defend her cubs, but one cub died after the encounter.

## How can I support Katmai’s bears?

Donations can be made to Katmai Conservancy’s Otis Fund. The Otis Fund is named after [Bear #480 (Otis)](https://katmaiconservancy.org/480-otis), who won four Fat Bear Week titles before his death around 2024.  All donations made between September 22 and October 3 will be matched by [explore.org](http://explore.org).

## What happened with the bears this summer?

This year’s livestream featured an example of how wild (and upsetting to humans) nature can be. On Tuesday, July 28, the live-cams captured a [young brown bear cub being killed and eaten by an unrelated mother bear](https://www.popsci.com/environment/bear-cub-killed-katmai-brooks-river-bear-806/) (Bear #806). The deceased cub was born this spring and the child of Bear #909, a 10-year-old brown bear. Bear #909 started the season with two cubs, but now lost both.

On Sunday, August 2, [one of Bear #335’s (Jolly) cubs died](https://www.popsci.com/environment/katmai-mother-bear-attacks-335-cub/), after following three unrelated cubs up a tree. The mother of the cubs already in the tree attacked Bear #335’s cub, who did not survive the encounter. The identity of the mother bear who killed the spring cub was not confirmed.

Following the first cub’s death, naturalist Mike Fitz and park rangers Christine Loberg and Sarah Bruce said this likely the first documented case occurring at Brooks River. While there is no one answer as to [why mother bears are killing cubs](https://www.popsci.com/environment/why-mama-bears-kill-cubs/), some experts suspect bear adoption, food scarcity, and fights for dominance all play a role.

Additionally, this year also saw a [cub with silver-hued fur](https://www.popsci.com/environment/silver-cub-spotted-katmai-bear-cam-alaska/), one cub who hopefully [learned important lesson about porcupine quill safety](https://www.popsci.com/environment/bear-cub-porcupine-quills-katmai-alaska/), the [unique fishing stylings of Bear #164](https://www.popsci.com/environment/meet-bucky-dent-one-of-katmais-most-innovative-fish-finder/) (Bucky Dent), Bear #284’s (Electra) family who can [“walk on water,”](https://www.popsci.com/environment/katmai-brown-bear-cubs-walk-water-alaska/) and even a few [cubs take a tumble over a waterfall](https://www.popsci.com/environment/katmai-bear-cubs-tumble-over-waterfall/).

The post [The Fat Bear Week 2026 bracket is here and chunkier than ever](https://www.popsci.com/environment/fat-bear-week-bracket-2026/) appeared first on [Popular Science](https://www.popsci.com).

entries.title: Manage the code coverage ruleset condition with the REST API
entries.content:
You can now use the generally available REST API to manage the `Restrict code coverage` repository ruleset option, in addition to the existing UI support.

This ruleset lets you enforce a minimum code coverage percentage based on line coverage or set a maximum tolerable coverage drop for a pull request. Previously, configuring this rule required using the web interface. Now you can create, update, and read this ruleset option programmatically, making it easier to manage code coverage requirements consistently across many repositories or as part of your existing infrastructure-as-code workflows.

To use this rule, your repository must have GitHub Code Quality enabled and code coverage uploads configured. It’s available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Team, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Learn more about [available rules for rulesets](https://docs.github.com/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets) and the [REST API endpoints for rules](https://docs.github.com/rest/repos/rules).

entries.title: GitHub Copilot weekly releases — September 14
entries.content:
This week, GitHub Copilot adds new model selection options, code review updates, and Sentry integration in the Copilot app. There are also updates for admins, plus new agent features in VS Code.

### [GitHub Copilot](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-18-github-copilot-weekly-releases-september-14#github-copilot)

* Copilot code review now resolves addressed comments during subsequent reviews, leaving outstanding feedback open. It also suggests commit messages when you apply its code suggestions. Reviews can use shell tools to validate changes, and Lite reviews now combine findings from multiple agents.
* Choose how Copilot weighs cost, quality, and response time with the new efficiency, balance, and intelligence tiers in auto model selection. All three tiers select from the same available models. This update is rolling out in VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the Copilot app.

### [GitHub Copilot Business and Enterprise users](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-18-github-copilot-weekly-releases-september-14#github-copilot-business-and-enterprise-users)

* Measure adoption and activity in the dedicated VS Code Agents window with new usage metrics that are now generally available. Enterprise and organization reports include daily active users, session counts, and user message totals, alongside user-level activity data. These metrics are separate from the editor-window metrics.
* Get help choosing values for repository custom properties with Copilot suggestions, now in public preview. For example, when you create an `internet-facing` property, Copilot can suggest `yes` and `no` as allowed values. Organization and enterprise owners can turn suggestions on or off through a Copilot policy.
* Request a higher Copilot budget from your organization or enterprise when you reach your AI credit limit. Owners and billing managers can approve, adjust, or deny requests in settings. Approval restores access to AI credits. This is now generally available for Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise plans with usage-based billing. This feature is not available for enterprises with managed users.

### [GitHub Copilot app](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-18-github-copilot-weekly-releases-september-14#github-copilot-app)

Fix production crashes from Sentry reports. Move from crash report to code fix with the new Sentry canvas in the GitHub Copilot app. Review errors, stack traces, and related context, then work with Copilot to investigate the cause, validate a fix, and prepare a pull request.

![The Customize window in the Copilot App with the Canvas tab selected. Three large boxes are featured, Azure DevOps, Sentry, and Jira. Each of them provides a title, description, and install button.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0095d7bd-0b8e-4caf-b7ba-664abb842ea7)

Download [the Copilot app](https://github.com/features/ai/github-app?utm_source=download-app-09-07&utm_medium=changelog&utm_campaign=weekly-copilot-launches-aug-2026).

### [VS Code 1.138 release updates](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-18-github-copilot-weekly-releases-september-14#vs-code-1-138-release-updates)

* Run agents with your project’s tools and dependencies using local Dev Containers in the Agents window. Support is rolling out gradually and requires both Docker and a supported Dev Container configuration.
* Automatically mark inactive sessions as **Done** once all their pull requests merge, with optional deletion after a separate grace period. Automatic cleanup is opt-in and now in preview.
* Create pull requests from Agent Host sessions without leaving the Agents window. Review the generated title and description, choose draft status, and create the pull request directly or ask your agent to do it.

Explore everything that’s new in the [full release notes](https://aka.ms/VSCode/138).

entries.title: FAA tees up $875M AI tool to help manage air traffic congestion
entries.content:
An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers on managing air traffic in the congested airspace above the Washington, DC, area. The expected launch would be the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the Federal Aviation Administration.

The FAA describes the [SMART system](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/SMART_One-Pager.pdf) as using AI models to predict air traffic flows and identify potential conflicts based on operational factors like airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. US government and industry officials told [The Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/business/airlines/the-faas-875-million-plan-to-use-ai-to-ease-air-traffic-woes-13107920) that SMART could debut for the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21.

The decision to launch SMART in limited scope before going nationwide is the “right call,” said Philip Mann, principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/09/faa-tees-up-875m-ai-tool-to-help-manage-air-traffic-congestion/)

entries.title: FCC lets Paramount sell 49.5% equity stake to Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Qatar
entries.content:
The Federal Communications Commission yesterday approved Paramount Skydance's plan to sell large equity stakes to the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar.

Under [US law](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/47/310), companies with licenses to run broadcast stations need FCC approval to have direct or indirect foreign ownership exceeding 25 percent of the company's stock. Paramount says its indirect foreign ownership will reach 49.5 percent after it receives investments from the sovereign wealth funds and filed a [petition](https://www.fcc.gov/ecfs/document/104272462615916/1) asking the FCC to waive the foreign ownership limit.

Paramount, the owner of CBS, holds FCC licenses for the 28 local CBS stations that it owns and operates. Paramount is buying Warner Bros. Discovery in a $111 billion deal that is being partially financed with foreign investment but hasn't completed the acquisition because US states filed a lawsuit that aims to block the merger. Trump's Department of Justice approved the merger.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/09/fcc-lets-paramount-sell-49-5-equity-stake-to-saudi-arabia-uae-and-qatar/)

entries.title: Finding the cells that put our brain to sleep
entries.content:
For a long time, sleep research has treated the cerebral cortex as a passive follower reacting to signals from the deep brain. “Usually, sleep is associated with being controlled by subcortical regions,” said Geoffrey Terral, a neuroscientist at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York.

The cortex is where the slow rhythms of deep sleep can be seen, but researchers assumed the signals that triggered them originated elsewhere. In a recent Nature study, Terral and Renata Batista-Brito, who runs the lab, report a population of cortical cells that challenges that assumption.

These cortical cells make up only around one percent of the cortex's inhibitory neurons, and switching them on in a mouse puts the animal to sleep. “What our work shows is that the cortex can not only see this rhythm but also initiate it by itself, and this is sufficient to promote sleep,” Terral said.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/09/finding-the-cells-that-put-our-brain-to-sleep/)

entries.title: The Best Gifts to Give an E-Book Reader
entries.content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

Unless you're shopping from a wishlist, buying a book for a big reader is always a fraught prospect. Have they read it? Will they like it? Will they be offended at the mere suggestion that you think it's the kind of book they might like? Will you be crushed when you give them a copy of your favorite book and they never get around to reading it?

Buying a gift for someone who prefers to read e-books—whether on a Kindle or [one of the many excellent non-Kindle alternatives](https://lifehacker.com/tech/best-e-readers-that-arent-a-kindle)—can be much less emotionally charged: Instead of risking everything by giving them a book, just get them a cute e-reader accessory (if not a new e-reader) that they will thank you for every time they dive into a good read.

## A truly pocketable travel e-reader: The Xteink X4 Pro

![THe Xteink X4 Pro next to a set of AirPods Pro 3 for scale](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/articles/01M2TN3X1HJF53C1CQCES0J4A7/images-2.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789751247.png)

Credit: Joel Cunningham

Chances are good your giftee already owns a Kindle, but there's room for another e-reader in their life—especially when it's as small as the [Xteink X4 Pro](https://zdcs.link/z6x6yl?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Xteink%20X4%20Pro&object_type=content&short_url=z6x6yl&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") ($99). TikTok and Reddit are obsessed with this tiny, quirky device from a Chinese tech startup that has taken the e-reading world by storm over the past year, and it's not hard to see why: For under $100, you can get a palm-sized, single-purpose e-ink device that will disappear into any pocket, so you can truly take your books with you wherever you go. (Promotional images even show it magnetically attached to the back of a smartphone.)

While the first Xteink device could be [clunky and cumbersome to use](https://lifehacker.com/tech/this-wallet-sized-e-reader-is-my-tech-upgrade-of-the-year), the new X4 Pro has improved software and quality-of-life updates like a faster processor, more RAM, a touchscreen, and a front light. It isn't the ideal primary device for every reader, but as an ultra-portable alternative for reading on the go, it's hard to beat—[though competitors have popped up to give it a go](https://lifehacker.com/tech/now-boox-is-making-a-tiny-e-reader-too). Learn more about the device (and its potential drawbacks) [in my full Xteink X4 Pro review](https://lifehacker.com/tech/xteink-x4-pro-review).

## An e-reader that can curb any smartphone addiction: The Boox Palma 2 Pro

If you've got more to spend and want to give a potentially transformative gift, consider the [Boox Palma 2 Pro](https://zdcs.link/QVJNZJ?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Boox%20Palma%202%20Pro&object_type=content&short_url=QVJNZJ&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") ($399.99), part of the family of phone-shaped devices that kicked off the small e-reader craze (and helped me kick my own doomscrolling habit). It has a 6.13-inch color e-ink screen and runs on an open Android operating system, which means it can connect to the Google Play Store and run any reading app, from Kindle to Nook. That means your giftee will be able to read all of their existing e-books wherever they're from, and get new ones from anywhere. It can connect to the internet via a mobile SIM and works with a stylus, so it also makes a great productivity and note-taking device, but with a screen that's easier on the eyes, less stimulating, and subsequently, much less addictive than a smartphone. ## A remote page turner: The Boox Tappy

![Boox Tappy next to a Boox Go 6](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/articles/01M2TN3X1HJF53C1CQCES0J4A7/images-1.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789751247.png)

Credit: Joel Cunningham

Typically, to turn pages on an e-reader, you have to press a button on the side of the device or, more often, tap the screen—but there's a better way: Bluetooth page turners connect to an e-reader and make it possible to turn the page by clicking a remote that you hold in your hand. This is obviously great for anyone with motor control issues, arthritis, or any disability that makes manipulating a screen difficult, but honestly, they can be pretty useful even if you don't experience anything of the sort. With a Bluetooth remote like the adorable [Boox Tappy](https://zdcs.link/QO6A38?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Boox%20Tappy&object_type=content&short_url=QO6A38&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") ($30), you can keep your hands under the blanket while you read with the e-reader propped in your lap, or enjoy a snack without worrying about getting Cheeto dust all over your touchscreen. My first reaction when testing one out was "this seems cute but unnecessary," but after a few reading sessions, I found it let me read more comfortably, no matter how I was sitting or what else I was doing.

Now for the bad news: Kindle devices don't support Bluetooth remotes. The list of compatible devices includes, well, basically any other kind of e-reader, whether one that runs on Android (like a Boox Go 6) or a Kobo like the Clara Colour (all Kobo devices support Bluetooth accessories). If your giftee has a Kindle, you'll need to get [a radio frequency remote](https://zdcs.link/9lxNer?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=a%20radio%20frequency%20remote&object_type=content&short_url=9lxNer&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") that turns pages by physically tapping the screen for you.

entries.title: Oregon’s data centers use almost 25% of the state’s power, report reveals
entries.content:
![Facebook's Prineville Data Center in Prineville, Oregon](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/03ypFj9BcFPN2eZq6ARPxWx/hero-image.jpg)

If you're not sure how you [feel](https://mashable.com/tech/trump-ai-data-centers-epa) about the [AI data center debate](https://mashable.com/article/ai-data-center-carbon-emissions-uk) yet, seeing news like this may just convince you that those [anti-data center folks](https://mashable.com/article/ai-data-center-moratorium) have a point.

In the first study of its kind since the [AI-driven data center discourse](https://mashable.com/tech/trump-ai-data-centers-epa) began, researchers in Oregon have [released a new report](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/09/17/oregon-data-centers-consume-quarter-state-power-report/) detailing the size of the data center industry in the state. In doing so, the researchers have also uncovered just how much energy data centers use up in the state.

SEE ALSO:
[Every U.S. state that bans data centers](https://mashable.com/tech/every-us-state-that-bans-data-centers)

According to the report, there are 111 operational data centers in the state of Oregon, which take up 22.1 million square feet of building space. Those data centers account for a whopping 23 percent of the state's entire retail energy sales in 2025.

The report also details that there are 32 additional data centers under construction or in the planning stages, which will take up an additional 6.9 million square feet.

The researchers behind the report believe that data center energy consumption in Oregon will rise to nearly 25 terawatt hours by 2030. That's around 31 to 32 percent of all electricity demand in the state and the same energy consumption as 2.5 million homes.

"Data center electricity demand is increasing substantially, and regional as well as state-level planning eﬀorts…indicate that accommodating large-load growth will require new electricity resources, transmission capacity, and coordinated infrastructure planning," the report says.

The report also found that these data centers directly employ 2,630 workers.

This new report was released on Thursday by ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia. It was funded by the entrepreneurship and environmentalist nonprofit Lemelson Foundation, which is based in Portland.

entries.title: How people are fighting back against Flock cameras
entries.content:
![ protest sign is seen next to Flock camera pole with the camera removed on East Crystal Falls Parkway in Leander on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, after the city canceled its contract with Flock Safety, which provides automatic license plate reader technology.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/020MNEovHoVDAVfXEUkiWq8/hero-image.jpg)

Flock cameras don’t look like much: a box on a pole, pointed at the road. But they photograph passing cars and turn where and when they were seen into searchable records. Police say that helps solve crimes. [Critics worry](https://mashable.com/tech/flock-cameras-explained-surveillance) about who can really search those records, what they can do with them, and how much of a person’s daily life they might reveal.

So what happens when people find one in their community and want it gone? Quite a bit, it turns out. Residents across the U.S. are mapping cameras, digging up contracts, and filling public meetings. Others have gone after the cameras themselves, [stealing](https://mashable.com/tech/winona-flock-cameras-stolen-minnesota) or [vandalizing them](https://mashable.com/tech/hackers-dismantle-flock-camera-to-see-how-it-works). And this week, [*404 Media*](https://www.404media.co/hackers-stole-flocks-camera-software-revealing-how-the-company-tracks-cars-and-people-2/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [*WIRED*](https://www.wired.com/story/hackers-flock-camera-data-shows-how-system-works/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) reported that hackers removed one and copied its stored data, giving journalists a rare look inside a device that features software capable of detecting people as well as cars.

Here’s a compilation of what people have done through maps, records requests, petitions, and city hall — and what those efforts have actually changed.

SEE ALSO:
[What are Flock cameras and why are they so controversial?](https://mashable.com/tech/flock-cameras-explained-surveillance)

## 1. Putting Flock cameras on the map

One way people are pushing back is by making the cameras easier to see. Volunteers with Deflock Maps, a crowdsourced automated license plate reader (ALPR) resource, [document license plate readers](https://mashable.com/tech/flock-camera-map-neighborhood) and add their locations to [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/). The site opens on a map dotted with numbered clusters of reported cameras. Search for a city or ZIP code, zoom in, and those clusters give way to individual locations. It includes readers made by Flock and other companies, though its volunteer-submitted data may be incomplete or out of date.

In San Francisco, 16-year-old Zachary Schwartz noticed there wasn’t a local DeFlock chapter, so he started one. [DeFlock SF](https://deflocksf.org/) pairs a city camera map with local news, a calendar of meetings about the technology, and a link for residents to contribute camera locations. Schwartz and fellow student Hugo Zorn have also made videos and spoken at [Police Commission meetings](https://sfstandard.com/pacific-standard-time/2026/09/18/pst-the-teens-fighting-flock-surveillance/). Schwartz has also [called for an audit](https://sfist.com/2026/09/16/deflock-sf-maps-local-cameras-spreads-awareness-about-flock-surveillance/) of how the city uses the cameras and what data they collect.

SEE ALSO:
[This map shows how many Flock cameras are in your neighborhood](https://mashable.com/tech/flock-camera-map-neighborhood)

DeFlock isn’t the only place people are documenting the technology. The Electronic Frontier Foundation’s [Atlas of Surveillance](https://www.atlasofsurveillance.org/) lets users search by city or police agency to see whether it has documented license plate readers. It answers a different question from DeFlock’s street-level map: which agencies have been identified as using the technology, rather than where each reported camera sits.

Curious what’s been documented near you? Enter your city or ZIP code in [DeFlock Maps](https://maps.deflock.org/) and zoom in on the numbered clusters to see individual camera locations. If you spot a reader that’s missing or marked incorrectly, [DeFlock explains how to add or correct it](https://deflock.org/app) through its app and OpenStreetMap. Just remember that a pin is a volunteer report, and an empty stretch of map isn’t proof there are no cameras.

## 2. Following the paper trail

Some people are fighting Flock by checking whether what happens behind the scenes matches what their city agreed to. In Syracuse, New York, [*Central Current* found](https://centralcurrent.org/syracuse-police-exposed-driver-data-to-thousands-of-cops-around-the-country/) a gap between the two. The city’s contract said its license plate data wouldn’t be shared outside the police department. But the department had granted access to other agencies, which police said was an accident. Over roughly a year, searches by officers around the country reached Syracuse’s data nearly 4.4 million times. And that wasn’t the only surprise in the paperwork. [*Central Current* also found](https://centralcurrent.org/why-flock-will-get-to-keep-syracuse-drivers-anonymized-data-even-if-lawmakers-cancel-their-contract/) that Flock could keep using Syracuse data after the contract ended.

When the city approved cameras from Axon to replace Flock’s, [Flock said](https://centralcurrent.org/syracuse-wants-to-break-up-with-flock-not-so-fast-company-says/) Syracuse couldn’t simply end its agreement early. It warned that the city might have to pay for both systems; so even as officials moved to replace the cameras, they faced questions about what Flock could do with the data and what the city might still owe.

People elsewhere have been looking at the searches themselves. The Electronic Frontier Foundation [examined Flock search logs](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/09/high-crime-lmao-how-cops-are-treating-mass-surveillance-joke/) released through public records requests and found that some users entered “LMAO” or “idk” as their reason for searching. And website [Have I Been Flocked?](https://haveibeenflocked.com/) puts released logs in one searchable place, though it has only the records it’s been able to obtain.

SEE ALSO:
[Have you been Flocked? This website lets you find out](https://mashable.com/tech/have-i-been-flocked-license-plate-search)

Curious what’s on record where you live? The American Civil Liberties Union ([ACLU) suggests](https://www.aclu.org/get-the-flock-out-toolkit) looking for Flock on city council agendas; you can also check Have I Been Flocked? for your local agency or request its search logs.

## 3. Showing up and organizing locally

For residents trying to push back against Flock cameras, the first step is often finding out who agreed to install them. From there, neighbors can compare what they’ve learned, organize around the next public meeting, and ask officials to make a decision in front of the people affected.

That’s what happened in Saranac Lake, New York. Cameras began appearing before many residents knew the village had agreed to install them, so they attended board meetings to ask who had approved the deal and why the public hadn’t been consulted. By a March meeting, [dozens had filled the room and the hallway](https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53141/20260311/saranac-lake-drops-plan-for-flock-surveillance-cameras-after-public-backlash). Trustees came prepared to pause the cameras while they wrote a policy. Residents argued for ending the program instead, and the board voted 4–1 to cancel the contract.

![The Muslim Justice League and other activists hold a protest in which they marched to Flock Safety offices in the Seaport on August 19, 2026](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/020MNEovHoVDAVfXEUkiWq8/images-1.fill.size_2000x1383.v1789755930.jpg)

An August protest against Flock in Boston, MA. 
Credit: Barry Chin/Getty Images

![Participants walk near the Gerald D. Hines Waterwall Park, stopping at several Flock Safety cameras along the way during a community walk led by Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, 27, and organized with Houston DSA and other groups in Houston, Saturday, Aug. 22, 2026.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/020MNEovHoVDAVfXEUkiWq8/images-2.fill.size_2000x1333.v1789755930.jpg)

Protesters rally in Houston during an August protest. 
Credit: Raquel Natalicchio/Getty Images

Elsewhere, people have kept the pressure on between meetings. In Milford, Connecticut, residents connected through a DeFlock Milford Facebook group, brought signs, and returned to speak as the debate continued. Activists even [projected "Flock Out Of CT" onto City Hall](https://www.ctinsider.com/news/article/milford-flock-cameras-aldermen-board-vote-22431340.php) before a vote. In Austin, [more than 30 community groups joined forces](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/06/victory-austin-organizers-cancel-citys-flock-alpr-contract) and residents raised concerns at a [council work session](https://www.kut.org/austin/2025-06-04/austin-tx-automatic-license-reader-program-police-data-privacy-flock) ahead of a decision on renewing the program.

If you want to find out what’s happening where you live, the [ACLU’s toolkit](https://www.aclu.org/get-the-flock-out-toolkit) can help you connect with a nearby group and identify which officials are the decision makers.

## 4. Writing lawmakers and gathering signatures

Not everyone can make it to a meeting. Some people are putting their objections in writing — and gathering thousands of signatures so officials can see how many others agree.

At the national level, the ACLU’s ["Get the Flock Out" campaign](https://action.aclu.org/send-message/get-flock-out) offers a draft message people can edit and send to members of Congress. It asks lawmakers to ban license plate readers. If they won’t, the message calls for limits on federal funding and use, warrants to access the data, and faster deletion.

> [This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.](https://twitter.com/ssyyllng/status/2099986800769196464 "(Opens in a new tab)")

Local petitions can name the people who have the power to remove specific cameras. In Texas, a [petition opposing Flock cameras in Boerne and Kendall County](https://www.change.org/p/remove-flock-cameras-from-boerne-and-kendall-county) asks county commissioners to cancel the agreement, take down the cameras, and delete the data they’ve collected.

Of course, a growing signature count doesn’t guarantee a changed vote. In Conroe, Texas, resident James Fletes [started a petition](https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/trending/article/conroe-city-council-backs-flock-safety-cameras-22352075.php) calling for the city to cancel its Flock contract. It had more than 1,200 signatures by July, but the council went on to shelve proposals to review the cameras or put their use to a public vote. (The city kept their Flock program.)

For people writing their own officials, the ACLU’s [organizing toolkit](https://www.aclu.org/get-the-flock-out-toolkit) has a sample email for state and local representatives, proposed rules for how camera data can be used and shared, and a resolution a city *could* use to cancel a Flock contract. Want to send something? You can personalize the [message to Congress](https://action.aclu.org/send-message/get-flock-out), or use the toolkit to make a specific request of the officials who control cameras where you live.

## 5. And yes, some people have gone after the cameras themselves

Some people have taken the fight to the cameras. In Houston, Flock readers have been found [damaged, painted, and knocked down](https://us4.campaign-archive.com/?u=79f27ae45ce3da6effd909ae7&id=ba4597d8c6). In another neighborhood, [four Flock cameras were cut down in late July](https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/article/flock-camera-sawed-old-braeswood-22370015.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com), prompting a law enforcement investigation. And in Winona, Minnesota, [all eight of the city’s police-operated Flock cameras were stolen](https://mashable.com/tech/winona-flock-cameras-stolen-minnesota). The people responsible haven’t necessarily explained their motives, but the incidents show how far the backlash has moved beyond public meetings.

![vandalized Flock camera near Washington Avenue and Westcott is photographed in Houston, Tuesday, July 7, 2026.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/020MNEovHoVDAVfXEUkiWq8/images-3.fill.size_2000x1249.v1789755930.jpg)

Credit: Raquel Natalicchio/Getty Images

![A vandalized Flock camera near Washington Avenue and Westcott is photographed in Houston, Tuesday, July 7, 2026.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/020MNEovHoVDAVfXEUkiWq8/images-4.fill.size_2000x1333.v1789755930.jpg)

Credit: Raquel Natalicchio/Getty Images

There are even people who went looking *inside* a Flock camera. Hackers removed one, copied the data stored on it, and shared the files with [*404 Media*](https://www.404media.co/hackers-stole-flocks-camera-software-revealing-how-the-company-tracks-cars-and-people-2/) and [*WIRED*](https://www.wired.com/story/hackers-flock-camera-data-shows-how-system-works/) this week. The journalists found software that could detect people as well as vehicles. Logs from the device showed it had generated about 1.6 million images of roughly 50,000 vehicles across 21 days of recoverable activity. Flock said removing and tampering with the camera was illegal.

The findings raise many questions: What can these devices detect? What data do they keep, and who can access it? If you’re wondering about cameras near you, start with the agency operating them and the officials who approved the contract.

SEE ALSO:
[Someone stole every Flock camera in this Minnesota city](https://mashable.com/tech/winona-flock-cameras-stolen-minnesota)

What the hackers found gives people more to ask about at the next public meeting. And those questions won’t disappear if a city swaps Flock for another company’s cameras, as Syracuse plans to do with Axon. We'll see where the fight goes, and how much more the public, and the company, can take.

The sale will run for 48 hours from Oct. 6 to 7 and compete with concurrent festivities at [Target](https://mashable.com/life/target-circle-deal-days-october-prime-day-2026) and [Walmart](https://mashable.com/life/walmart-october-prime-day-deals-2026).

Prime Big Deal Days will be an opportunity to get a head start on your [Black Friday](https://mashable.com/category/black-friday) wishlist — and to get some relief from the [RAMageddon price hikes](https://mashable.com/tech/ramageddon-every-tech-price-increase-2026) impacting the tech industry this year. ## Release Notes

Released on 2026-09-18.

### Enhancements

* Reject unsupported Git archive paths in lockfiles with a clear error instead of panicking during frozen exports ([#21780](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21780))

### Preview features

* Set minimum glibc and musl versions that universal resolutions must support with `minimum-libc-version` ([#21651](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21651))
* Reject `pylock.toml` files whose wheel filenames do not match their declared package names or versions ([#20746](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/20746))
* Keep `uv workspace metadata` read-only unless `--sync` is provided ([#21821](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21821))
* Apply `uv check` lock modes when retrieving workspace metadata ([#21821](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21821))

### Performance

* Speed up builds with many exclusion patterns by avoiding quadratic deduplication ([#21650](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21650))
* Reduce resolver allocations when deduplicating package and distribution requests ([#21810](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21810))

### Bug fixes

* Prevent `required-environments` from selecting package versions whose wheels require a newer macOS version than the configured Darwin baseline ([#21825](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21825))

### Documentation

* Clarify the 0.12.14 and 0.12.15 release notes ([#21817](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21817))

## Install uv 0.12.17

### Install prebuilt binaries via shell script

```
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://releases.astral.sh/github/uv/releases/download/0.12.17/uv-installer.sh | sh
```

### Install prebuilt binaries via powershell script

```
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://releases.astral.sh/github/uv/releases/download/0.12.17/uv-installer.ps1 | iex"
```

entries.title: Will California Gut Its Net Neutrality Law to Comply with Trump Admin Demands?
entries.content:
In 2021, America approved $65 billion to fund broadband internet services as part of President Biden's Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. But Trump's administration announced they'd withhold funds from states with net neutrality protections...
States could object and sue the government, Ars Technica reported last October, "but even a successful lawsuit could take years and leave unserved homes without broadband for the foreseeable future." So where does that leave California's net neutrality laws? Ars Technica asks. California expect to spend about $1.4 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations...
Similar to federal net neutrality rules repealed during the first Trump administration, California's law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. While the first Trump administration lost its attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, the second Trump administration is trying to achieve a similar result by making federal broadband money conditional on whether states agree not to enforce net neutrality...
California and Illinois are the only states that haven't finalized their funding, according to the BEAD progress dashboard maintained by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA)... California could try to continue enforcing its net neutrality law even while accepting the federal funding, a strategy that would involve another long court battle over its right to regulate broadband providers. This would be difficult, as the Trump administration is requiring states that accept grant funding to commit that they won't enforce net neutrality rules... [N]early 30 advocacy groups that focus on access to technology are treating the vote as a significant milestone and urged state leaders to defend California's net neutrality law in a letter yesterday...
Winning a court battle would become much more difficult after the state accepts the money [according to Paul Goodman, legal counsel for the Center for Accessible Technology]. Goodman said the CPUC should delay the vote and that California should file a lawsuit arguing that the NTIA-imposed condition is illegal. In addition to net neutrality, Goodman said California may be giving up other regulatory authority over companies, like AT&T and Verizon, because the NTIA requirement forbids rate regulation and "utility-style rules on broadband Internet service" in general... Goodman said the exemption from state laws would last for up to 14 years. This is because ISPs receiving grants would have four years to deploy the required broadband networks, and the extended period of performance lasts another 10 years... AT&T is already trying to get out of state obligations related to its basic phone service in California, as we've reported... [Also at stake is whether "ISPs themselves get to pick the price of the mandated low-cost broadband offerings," the article points out.]
The letter from 30 advocacy groups to California state leaders argues accepting the money "would set a dangerous precedent for the federal government to use federal funding as a cudgel that forces states in line with its agenda... If California were to allow this funding to be used as leverage, there is no telling what other resources the administration would confidently seek to exploit."
Thursday California's Public Utility Commission did vote to approve the plan, but a spokesperson earlier told Ars Technica their vote "does not address subgrantee agreements, or the conditions the NTIA requires be included in subgrantee agreements."

[![](https://a.fsdn.com/sd/twitter_icon_large.png)](http://twitter.com/home?status=Will+California+Gut+Its+Net+Neutrality+Law+to+Comply+with+Trump+Admin+Demands%3F%3A+https%3A%2F%2Fyro.slashdot.org%2Fstory%2F26%2F09%2F18%2F0023251%2F%3Futm_source%3Dtwitter%26utm_medium%3Dtwitter)
